newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala conference focuses on murdered journalists.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala conference focuses on murdered journalists.

text.p: At least 169 journalists were murdered in the Americas in the last seven years and almost none of the deaths have been solved, the Interamerican Press Association (IAPA) said on Wednesday.
The IAPA will draw attention to the unpunished murders of reporters at its annual meeting, which gathered publishers from across the hemisphere in Guatemala City for three days.

"The IAPA is very concerned about any attacks on journalists," IAPA president Luis Gabriel Cano, of Colombia, told Reuters. "We investigate each case thoroughly and then make a pronouncement to let the whole world know."
The IAPA's Press Freedom Commission will issue a report on "Unpunished Crimes against Journalists," based on a two-year study of six killings in Colombia, Mexico and Guatemala.
Colombian President Ernesto Samper and his predecessor Cesar Gaviria, now Secretary General of the Organisation of American States, were due to attend the conference.

Investigators and relatives of the six dead journalists will speak to the meeting and a panel will pass a moral judgment on the presumed killers, who are suspected of being drug traffickers, army personnel or government agents.

The IAPA has not established who committed the murders. Instead it focused on exposing faulty investigations and showing how government indifference and intimidation against judges hampered resolution of the six killings.

"We have shown in these six cases a very sad story. In almost all of the cases, the governments have done almost nothing," David Lawrence, editor of the Miami Herald and a former IAPA president said in an interview.

The six journalists were Colombians Guillermo Cano Isaza, murdered in 1986, and Carlos Lajud Catalan, killed in 1993; Guatemalans Jorge Carpio Nicolle, kiled in 1993, and Irma Flaquer Azurdia, who disappeared in 1980; and Mexicans Hector Felix Miranda, killed in 1988, and Victor Manuel Oropeza, murdered in 1991.

The IAPA meeting will also issue a statement on the case of Baruch Izcher, an Israeli-born television station owner whose Peruvian citizenship was revoked after his station aired a report on phone tapping by Peru's security services.

Press Freedom Commission president Danilo Arbilla, editor of the Uruguayan business weekly Busqueda, went to Peru to investigate the Izcher case and will report back to the IAPA executive commitee on Thursday.
